entry.title: Intro to Deep Learning using Pytorch

link.title: Intro to Deep Learning using Pytorch

entry.content:
• Learning Objectives
  • What is Deep Learning
  • Simple Feedforward Networks
  • U-Net
  • Objectives

The motivation for this post is to elucidate the basic of deep learning to myself. If any others benefit from this post, then that is always a plus. I will using Russell and Norvig 4e as the source material along with anything that I find useful in Deep Learning by Ian Goodfellow.

Learning Objectives

I hope to focus on what a robotics engineering focusing on robotic manipulation would need. This lens should sufficiently distinguish my post from others and make it most apt for my needs.

  1. Define what deep learning is.
  2. Construct a couple models focused on robotics applications.
  • U-Net
  • Transformer
  • Variational Auto-Encoder
  • LSTM
  • Diffusion Model
  1. Explain the design choices behind each of the models chosen.

What is Deep Learning

For a roboticist, deep learning provides a convenient way to develop algorithms for performing complex manipulation tasks that would normally be impossible because there are too many factors and scenarios for the ordinary programmer to consider. Therefore, roboticist opt for machine learning methods where they can take a set of data and then have a robot “learn” an algorithm (ie a set of instructions given a specific program state or value of a variable”). More specifically, we develop a template program with a bunch of knobs that can be turned to produce the result we want. Here we tune or “learn” the program by running the data through the template program and then compare it to the results that we expect it to have. This means we need to have data that also includes the expect prediction in order for us to compare it with what our model outputs. In some ways, this is similar to debugging where we have a program and we run it to see what it outputs and then we will tweak it until we get the output we expect. The difference is that we are typing in a programming language (ie code) whereas when we learn an algorithm, the computer is thinking in terms of weights. It’s important to remember that when we program, we are really working with numbers and when we program in human readable programming language then we are really performing mathematical operations on numbers. This is a brief overview of machine learning and I would suggest looking online for more information as there is a plethora of materials available on the Internet.

Now let’s get into deep learning! Deep learning is a type of machine learning that uses complex algebraic circuits with tunable connection strengths 1. Deep learning a method where we do algorithm tuning mentioned earlier but we focus on doing it in a certain way. In deep learning where stack a bunch of “layers” together to perform a very complex transformation on the data that will generate a prediction based on our input. There’s a lot there so let’s break it down. We start with what is called a neural network which a big collection of these functions called neurons that take an input value in and then pass them through a function to produce a transformation o the data. We can do this process multiple times and this results in a very complex math function that we wouldn’t have been able to come up with on our own. The network here indicates that part of the input or output to one function can be used to affect the input or output of other functions so all these functions have an effect on each other, hence the name network. The neural part of the name is synonymous with the neural cells in our brains because they take an input value in and the produce some output value that is passed along to another function in a chain 2. This process is an algorithm because we put the input through the beginning of the neural network and then it will procedurally go through a series of transformations to generate a prediction or output. This type of programming is different than traditionally programming because we don’t really know what the tuning up or down for a function in a network does besides whether the whole network predicts better or worse. So we use the value of whether the network predicts worse or better to tune some functions up or down automatically using an optimizer function. We say that the model predicts worse or better using a loss function which is just the number we calculate to tell us whether our model is performing how we want or not. Generally, this number is how far off our prediction is or the number of wrong predictions but we can choose to calculate other numbers as well. The relevance of this number will have a strong effect on whether our model does a good job or not.

Simple Feedforward Networks

U-Net

Objectives

This intro post is focused on providing a succint tutorial on how to use pytorch based on the tutorial already available on the pytorch tutorials page. I will try to explain it further so there is additional explanation for why we do certain things and how they can be repurposed.

I have included the jupyter notebook below to make it easier to follow along. This is just a static display of the code and if you want more details, as always feel free to drop a comment or email me and I’ll try to get back to you.

In order to build a basic ML pipeline using Pytorch, you follow the basic architecture below.

Before you start, you want to make sure you have a dataset in mind along along with all the relevant considerations like how you want to split it for training, validation, and testing. You may want to inspect the data to see what kind of architecture would best fit it. If you are dealing with images for example, it might be best to use a U-Net which is a type of Convolutional Neural Net (CNN).

First, you import all your libraries. So you will need to import torch and make sure that your python points to the right direction. You can choose to import the submodules within pytorch directly into the script (eg from torch import nn) or type the full name out (eg torch.nn).

Second, you subclass the nn.Module base class and build whatever model you want. In this case, we named it a generic name, NeuralNet, although if it’s a specific model then be more specific. When subclassing nn.Module, make sure to call super().__init__(). You will also need to define a forward method so you can train the model. You can add hooks and extra things as well that will be called everytime you run a forward pass on a model training. In this case, we define a basic neural net that uses a series of linear transforms with ReLU activation functions. This is one of the most simple Deep Learning models we can make and it is an example of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or Feedforward Neural Network.

We basically flatten the input, an image, into a 1D vector and then pass it through a series of linear transformations that will be tuned using an optimizer and loss function. We lose 2D spatial relationships between neighboring pixels when we flatten the input image but it makes the model very simple. We dealing with more complex images than the FashionMNIST dataset which is black and white, we will consider using more complex models.

Third, we define a way to train the model using the training data we decided before starting. Pytorch comes with a dataloader but there are other libraries that also provide dataloaders for model training like huggingface_hub. We define the training loop by setting a batch size (ie how many images we want to run through the model before deciding whether we should increase or decrease the weights of some or every model parameter). We set the batch size and make sure every tensor/vector is on the same computing device (ie gpu). We run the input through the model and compare the model prediction with the correct prediction. Then we run the optimization function to update the model’s weights/params.

We will define something similar for the testing function, except we remove all the logic to update the weights.

Fourth, we implement the whole program logic to run the previous steps we previously mentioned so that our program has a place to start and a set of steps to actually follow. Before, we were just defining a bunch of classes and functions.

Finally, after we trained our model, we can run the model on our compute and see what it says on a new result that may or may not be in our dataset.

entry.title: Realisation about progress in research
entry.content:
I’m making this post so that I can continue to get in the habit of writing something that I will publish daily. I know that it’s not as polished or technical as I would like it to be, but with the clock reaching 10:30pm, I figured something is better than nothing.

I wanted to write this post about how I realized that one of the major blockers in my research is the fact that it is so easy to cook up a dream of success and that letting it go is both extremely humbling and freeing. I find that it is part of a greater message of learning to be active and present in the current moment rather than thinking about castles in the sky 1. I realized this after talking with a close friend and mentor and decided that I would try something different. I decided that I would try to let go of my expectations for work today and just focus on trying to just make good, simple choices.

I know that everything I’ve mentioned seems obvious, but as an aspiring researcher, it’s a lesson that I’m beginning to learn firsthand. I’ve got a lot to talk about and explain on this blog and by practicing this habit daily even with posts like this, I hope to publicly make progress in developing useful technical reports that others can make great use of.

Tomorrow I hope to write a post about diffusion models and explain them based on the amazing post by Lillian Weng on Diffusion Models, Julia Turc’s video on Diffusion Models, a tutorial video by DeepFindr, and some others.

entry.title: Diffusion Policy
entry.content:
• Diffusion Models

This is my first technical post and I think it will be a good open to later discussions about how to implement decision-making and control algorithms 1. I will be heavily relying on the paper released by Cheng et al 2024 and a post by Lillian Weng on Diffusion Models.

I will start off by explaining what a diffusion policy is. A diffusion policy is a visuomotor policy for robotic manipulation based on the popular Diffusion Model which is used for image generation (think Stable Diffusion, etc.) 2. Diffusion policies were popularized by Cheng et al who uses them for Imitation Learning (IL) in comparison to popular alternatives like Iterative Behavior Cloning (IBC) which use the ideas behind implicit/energy-based models.

This post will be focused on diffusion policies for manipulation because I’m currently working on research to use diffusion policies for garment folding. Okay, that’s not the only reason, I also want to use this as an attempt to start writing regularly again after I mentioned it in my last post.

My plan in this post is to outline an implementation strategy for testing and getting a feel for a diffusion policy. I want this post to somewhat comprehensive so it will require that I first start with Diffusion Models.

Diffusion Models

Diffusion policies serve as a method for implementing visuomotor policies for robotic manipulation 2.

  1. I’ve found there’s not a clear distinction between decision-making and control algorithms, especially in the robotics space. I like the distinction found in Game AI where decision-making refers to high level search and planning algorithms, often operating at the semantic level, while control refers to low-level search and planning algorithms.  ↩

  2. A visuomotor policy is a way to formulate a state space where we can have images as states and then have movement/joint-commands/etc. as actions to transition between states (i.e. when I move I should see a new image and that new image is caused exclusively by my previous action.) This means that we should be able to model static environment fairly well since the only way to see something is by performing an action like moving the robot forward.  ↩ ↩2

entry.title: FoldNet and FoldNet++
entry.content:
• What are they doing?
  • Why do I think this is useful?
  • How does this contribute to my research?

This post is a review of the FoldNet and FoldNet++ papers.

What are they doing?

They develop an extensive synthetic dataset for T-shirt folding and unfolding (ie getting clothes into a flattened stated from an arbitrarily crumbled state). They generate T-shirt meshes with semantic keypoint annotations and then use a rule-based manipulation framework (ie heuristic) to fold and unfold clothes from abitrary configurations. They evaluate various model types like vision-action models (e.g. visuomotor policy), vision-action-language models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs), in both sim and real-world evaluation environments. They achieve over 90% end-to-end task success rates on arbitrary initial garment states.

They note that they are able to get better performance compared to alternative techniques like action primities (a traditional technique), model-based techniques which try to model garment dynamics to plan actions, and end-to-end manipulation policies using behavior cloning which has become a more popular technique in recent years.

Why do I think this is useful?

They outline a strategy for training a policy without the need for expensive human demonstrations common in behavior cloning approaches. By using the their pipeline for simulated data, it’s possible to create a complete end-to-end model training pipeline by running a simulation, getting hundreds of thousands of samples with the option to run domain randomization, and then training a model of choice to obtain a manipulation policy.

How does this contribute to my research?

This contributes to my research by providing a potential data source and methodology for training a model to autonomously fold and unfold clothes. I would need to obtain their trained weights and then see if I can improve the 90% task success rate by adjusting the model or seeing how it performs on other types of clothes or configurations. I could combine it with other publicly available datasets to make a better trained model.

entry.title: Garment Folding Feature Representation
entry.content:
This post is a bit of a rush job so I hope to come back and polish it up, but its more important that I just get a post out if I want to keep this habit up.

I spent some time today writing notes about the different ways that researchers have used to represent the feature space for garment folding tasks. I am still working on going through the different types of methods but the main ones that I have noticed are image based (RBG-D), mesh-based, keypoints, semantic keypoints, implicit representation, learned latent space, and a new deformation aware reprentation using a temporal constrastive pretraining approach. The last one is latest and the authors compare it with a similar point-based approach used by the authors of UniGarmentManip.

The main thing that I learned from taking these notes is the feature representation can have a major impact on the training stability, performance, and generalizability of a model. In order to create fast, high performance models, it’s important to get the feature representation right and this design choice must work with the model architecture to create a good performance. One of the other considerations that I noticed is that some features are easier to obtain in simulation than in real-life so its important to select features that can be easily obtained.

If the proposed data pipeline and model require that real-world data be used then its important to account for the fact that some features may have error that can cause the model training to experience drift because the features are temporally related and so they may make it harder to model the features and deploy for autonomous operation in the real-world.

Instant-Fold is one of the latest papers that uses a masked RBG-D observation which is passed into a frozen DINO model to obtain an image embedding. Simulataneously, the depth image is converted into a point cloud and sampled. The samples of 3D points are projected on the image embedding using a bilinear interpolation. Once the 3D points are projected onto the image embedding, both the 3D position data and the image embedding from the DINO model are passed into a MLP to produce a 3D token representation. The process is how the pretraining is completed.

Another approach is to directly use the RBG-D images and pass them into Spatial Action Maps. This approach is used by Speedfolding and APS-Net (Zhou et al 2025). Speedfolding uses the Spatial Action Maps to classify an action primitive and predict parameterizations of the action primitives (ie we select whether to pick & place, fling, or drag and then specify two planar gripper locations that the robot arms should be in to perform the task). APS-Net is similar but they also collect keypoints on the garment to determine if the garment is sufficiently smooth. These approaches work fairly well with success rates around the 80% range but it seems the lack the kind of generalization and robustness that a model should have in order to be deployed in the real-world.

Diffusion Policies are being chosen over Spatial Action Maps due to the fact that they can better represent multi-modal action distributions compared to explicit policy representations like Spatial Action Maps. Diffusion Policies also have better training stability and robustness and they have nice properties like the assumption that we are sampling from an action distribution created from the training data.

entry.title: How to build a simple diffusion model

link.title: How to build a simple diffusion model

entry.content:
I am basing this post off of a video (diffusion model tutorial) generated by Zachary Huang.

A diffusion policy can formulated various different ways, although the most popular formulation is as a DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabalistic Model). It carefully adds noise to a sample from the prediction distribution until it resembles random noise. Then we will try to teach a neural network to predict the noise that was added. Lastly, we will start with a sample of random noise and then get the neural network to predict the noise until we get to a sample from the prediction distribution that we tried to estimate using the neural network.

We create the following classes to construct a basic diffusion model:

  • DiffusionConfig: holds all the different configuration values that we want to pass to the diffusion model we want to train.
  • SinusoidalPositionalEmbeddings: contains a way to embed the timestep t 1 that we are on while denoising the random noise into a sample from the predicted distribution. This uses the same trick as Transformers.
  • UNetBlock: construct a class to hold the sequence of transformations within a U-Net block/layer. We want it to take in the image and the timestep.
  • SimpleUNetModel: contains the forward training method for training a UNet model using the UNetBlock class. We will use this as the noise predictor.
  • DiffusionModel: class to noise the images from our training data using our DiffusionConfig class. We can use a reparameterization trick to instantly compute the value of the diffusion process at any timestep. We also define forward and sample methods. The forward method is a method for training the model. The sample method is used to obtain a random noise sample and then denoise it into a sample from the prediction distribution. The sample method is what we will call after we have a trained model offline 2 to generate predictions.

[Single Forward Diffusion Step]

The forward process in Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) adds Gaussian noise to a data sample $x_0$ over $T$ steps according to a variance schedule $\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots, \beta_T$. The reparameterization trick allows sampling $x_t$ at an arbitrary time step $t$ directly from $x_0$ in closed form without iteratively sampling through all intermediate steps.

(1)

\[x_{t} = \sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\epsilon\]

where $x_t$ is the current noisy sample we predict using the previous noised sample $x_{t-1}$. $\alpha_t$ is the signal percentage and $\beta_t$ is the noise percentage. Both alpha and beta must obviously sum to 1.

This equation gives us the value of the noised sample after T timesteps, but in order to calculate T noise iterations over the original sample $x_0$ we recursively compute this value T times. For example, if we want to compute 500 timesteps, we would need to compute that equation 500 times in order to get the noised sample value at timestep T=500.

We can derive an equation to compute the noised sample at any timestep t by using the reparameterization trick. The way we derive this is by taking the equation above where $x_{t-1} is the original state of the sample from the training data and $x_t$ is the state after we add a little noise, ie. $x_1$.

Expressing $x_{t-1}$ using the same definition:

(2) \(x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}} x_{t-2} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_{t-1}} \epsilon_{t-2}, \quad \text{where } \epsilon_{t-2} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\)

Substituting $x_{t-1}$ into the equation for $x_t$:

(3) \(x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t} \left( \sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}} x_{t-2} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_{t-1}} \epsilon_{t-2} \right) + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t} \epsilon_{t-1}\)

(4) \(x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}} x_{t-2} + \sqrt{\alpha_t (1 - \alpha_{t-1})} \epsilon_{t-2} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t} \epsilon_{t-1}\)

Recall that for two independent Gaussian random variables $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_1^2 \mathbf{I})$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_2^2 \mathbf{I})$, their linear combination yields:

(5) \(X + Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2) \mathbf{I})\)

So if we say $A = \sqrt{\alpha_t (1 - \alpha_{t-1})} \epsilon_{t-2}$ and $B = \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t} \epsilon_{t-1}$:

  • Variance of $A$: $\alpha_t (1 - \alpha_{t-1})$ (refer to eqn 4)
  • Variance of $B$: $1 - \alpha_t$ (refer to eqn 4)

Summing the variances gives:

(6) \(\sigma_{\text{combined}}^2 = \alpha_t (1 - \alpha_{t-1}) + (1 - \alpha_t) = \alpha_t - \alpha_t \alpha_{t-1} + 1 - \alpha_t = 1 - \alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}\)

Therefore, the combined noise term can be written as a single scaled Gaussian noise vector $\sqrt{1 - \alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}} \bar{\epsilon}{t-2}$, where $\bar{\epsilon}{t-2} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})$:

(7) \(x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}} x_{t-2} + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}} \bar{\epsilon}_{t-2}\)

Therefore, we can use the additivity of variance property which says if we have two uncorrelated distributions then we add the variances together. Secondly, we assume Gaussian distributions that have a mean of 0 which means we can use a simplified equation for adding the variances together, $Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)$. We want to multiply the variances together which can be derived from the additivity of variance property as a special case. So we can easily multiply the independent, zero mean Gaussian distribution variances to return the variance of the noised sample at timestep T.

(8) \(\bar{\alpha}_{T}=\prod_{i=0}^{T} (1- \beta_i)\) where $\beta_i$ is the variance at that iteration given by the variance schedule that we decide. Remember $\alpha_i=(1-\beta_i)$.

All of this means that when we try to solve for $x_{500}$, for example, we can say $\bar{\alpha}{500}=\prod{i=0}^{500} (1-\beta_i)$

[Reparameterization Trick]

(9)

\[x_t = \sqrt{\bar{a_t}}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{a_t}}\epsilon\]

where $x_0$ is a sample from our training data, $\epsilon$ is a random noise sample, and $x_t$ is a noisy sample at timestep t.

Alpha represents the signal strength while beta represents the noise strength. We can adjust the beta to increase or decrease the signal strength since they must both sum to 1. We square the values of alpha and beta in the equation above so the variances sum to 1. $\alpha_t + \beta_t = 1$ $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must sum to 1.

Reverse Diffusion Step

Given a noisy image, is it possible to estimate what the unnoised image was? Reversing the diffusion step is mathematically intractable because it means we must run each forward pass over the entire dataset in order to figure out which image noise was added to.

When trying to perform the reverse diffusion step, we predict the original sample by rearranging the reparameterization formula so we can solve for $x_0$. We already know the $x_t$ and if we can predict the noise, $\epsilon$ then we can compute the $x_0$. In order to predict $\epsilon$, we need to select a model that can take a random noise sample and then return an output of the same dimension given a specific timestep. A common model used for applications where we have the same size input and output is the U-Net model.

So we will call our U-Net the noise predictor model and it will take a noisy image and timestep t and then return the predicted noise which will have the same shape as the noisy image. We denote this as:

\[\epsilon_0(\mathbf{x}_t,t) \approx \epsilon\] 
graph LR;
  A((Noisy Image x_t)) --> C[U-Net: epsilon_0]
  B{Timestep t} --> C
  C --> D((Predicted Noise))
\[x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a_t}}(x_t - \frac{1-a_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{a_t}}}\epsilon_0) + \sigma_t\bar{z}\]

where $x_t$ is the current noisy sample and $x_{t-1}$ is a sample that is slightly cleaner than $x_t$. $\bar{\alpha_t}$ is just the cumulative product of the $\alpha_t$ over every timestep we are trying to cover.

This equation can be derived by taking the single forward diffusion step function and inputting the next x_t. So for the first iteration of that equation we have $

Loss Function

\[L=MSE(\epsilon,epsilon_0)\]

where $\epsilon$ is the real noise in the image and $\epsilon_0$ is the predicted noise from our UNet Model.

So far we have calculated the forward diffusion process along with a reparameterization trick, found a way to estimate the reverse diffusion process, and now we can use the loss function to update our model weights for tuning a function to predict the noise in a noisy image. We have the ground truth label (ie the noise $\epsilon$ from our training data) and we have the prediction from the model. So we have everything we need to compute the MSE (mean squared error).

Once we compute the loss (MSE), then we can use an optimizer like SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent) to update the model weights.

Sinusoidal Positional Embeddings

  1. Some researchers also call this the iteration step ↩

  2. Offline means assume the model will operate in the same prediction range as our training data. We are not able to update the model without retraining it completely on the new data. Online means that we can update our model as we receive new data. ↩

entry.title: Intro to the Modern Python Development Environment

link.title: Intro to the Modern Python Development Environment

entry.content:
Goal

The goal of this essay is to enable the reader to be able to establish a baseline understanding as to code reproducibility in programming and the necessity for creating environments that can be deployed on any platform that may be included in the deployment audience. Additionally, this essays covers the use of tools designed for creating elegant and professional looking code that can be easily transferred from drawing to code and tested to meet performance criteria. This essay is a basic introduction into the principles that guide modern development with an implementation in the Python language. An effort will be make to ensure that this can be applied to other languages when possible.

Assumptions that I need to address

  1. OS principles:
  2. Unix style file directory
  3. OS processes

  4. How is the computer broken down:

    The computer is broken down into a kernel that connects the hardware with the applications and services that you want to run. The following picture illustrates the point:

We see that the hardware is all connected to the kernel, in this case Linux kernel, and it will make sure that all the services inside and above can talk to the list of daemons, shells, toolkits, etc. can have resources. Think of it like a broker service.

Essay

The goal of this essay is to enable the reader to be able to understand what problems that professional developers, specifically in the context of python developers face. This is for a more general audience as different python developers can varying problems based on their application such as optimization challenges or package management problems. There are more comprehensive ways to cover these and they require a lot of discourse to fully unpack (the unintended pun being that packages are unpacked to have access to their classes, functions, and methods). This essay will cover what problems developers run in the implementation of their ideas into code and the what solutions are used to solve these problems. This is not specific to computer scientists, rather these principles affect all people who perform technical work in the coming years as programming proficiency has developed into an almost universal requirement for any STEM disciplines.

The problems that people run into programming generally is code reproducibility, Code Maintenance, Code communication, and code comprehension. The solutions are then applied to these categories based on popularity, ease of use, and applicability. First, code reproducibility problems occur when someone tries to hand another person code and they are not able to set your computer up like theirs. Second, Code Maintenance problems occur when code must be utilized over a period of time outside of immediate use which leads to the problems of making sure the infrastructure still supports the operation of your code. This is especially relevant after some code needs to reconfigured to operate a different way or have additional functionality.

Note: that code reproducibility and Code Maintenance are very closely linked which is why it is important that great care is taken in making sure that programs are developed in well organized environments almost like lab experiments.

Third, Code communication is when more than one person is working on code then how do you make sure that your change won’t screw up the codebase. Consider the fact that multiple people may be working on different functions that are going to placed in the same document. How can you make sure that the solution that you’ve made still works? Fourth and lastly, code comprehension problems occur when people are unable to understand the code they are presented because it is too complex, foreign, or proper documentation is not available.

code reproducibility in the modern world involves using dependencies. This is simply a fact that one must accept since the code you develop will always rely on some other part that must be trusted and understood to whatever degree the application requires. Fortunately, this problem can be documented such that similar to citing you sources; you can specify your dependencies so others can analyze and recreate your work. The issue with code reproducibility is version control for dependencies which is an important problem that requires the use of solutions like package management tools like poetry and Conda for Python. Understanding how to set up and implement dependency management tools and environment management for Python is a topic that can be addressed in a separate article. The second code reproducibility issue is managing environment variable which is crucial for SSH scripting. This is particularly important for a language like Python which has a fair bit of interaction with the CLI (Command Line Interface). The CLI is used to How to start up conda environments|start up conda environments, how to activate package scripts|activate package scripts like Sphinx package (a documentation generator for Python) or poetry for package management. Using tools like Docker can alleviate this problem since it creates a containerization|container that will utilize all the same OS processes as your computer; however, it will create a completely new Unix style file directory and environment variables list. The third issue is file directory setup which is solved by Docker. This means that the way your file explorer or finder app shows your computers file directory is the same. Having a standard file directory is a big problem when your program is trying to figure out what it is running on and use dependencies and information from that computer to run well. Consider where the program should store data or what if it references another file. If you open up Steam then it shows all the games you have, but what if you move the files for your games somewhere else around the computer then it will not be able to find it. You could probably trick your computer by replacing a file with a black file that has the same name and changing the name of the original file. This is a surefire way to have many problems stop working. This assumption that I can find files and data around your computer is crucial for complex problems that involve user interaction. Consider the environment variables list mentioned earlier. This list must be stored somewhere and depending on your OS the location may be different.

Code Maintenance is another major issue that some would argue would fall under reproducibility though I focused more on how the code needs to be maintained over time when changes are made or it is modified. Unfortunately, code is similar to a house blueprint where you can modify the drawing after it is finished but then it may affect other parts in ways that you don’t expect. Consider the following two images:

When you add a mustache to the Mona Lisa the have made the picture less cohesive and this can clutter up as you manipulate a program beyond it’s designed functionality.

This should be balanced with the DRY principle which says “Don’t Repeat Yourself” ie. try to abstract ideas that repeatedly used into little pieces that you can reuse over an over when you need. This doesn’t mean you turn everything into a perfect pieces. Rather, find stuff that you are doing in a tedious and repetitive way and see if programming it saves you any time. Many times its easier to let it go and not program unless you enjoy it. Creating well maintained, reusable code is a way to make your life easier in the future, especially if the code will be used often or flexibly.

Enough justification about Code Maintenance, now it’s time explain some of the types of problems and how they are solved. The main problems that developers face in Code Maintenance is Code Abstraction, code refactorization, and code testing. These three problems are found in the fact that making general solutions to programming problems is hard and oftentimes it’s easy to hardcode or pile things up into one file rather than abstract code into something general.

Code Abstraction is when you try to develop abstract representations of your code such as putting a set of commands into a function, class, or script. This means that whenever a set of code does some set of commands then it should be turned into a function. That function can then placed into larger functions such that a more complex feature is executed. Another approach is to use class and then attach methods so that if you have a class then it will contain all the stuff it needs to operate. Have a set of classes then you can put them together into a larger class that will contain all those functions and whatever else it needs.

Code Modularity is a concept that allows you to tuck away the details and trust that the solution works when you apply it. Then the only work is about how you use your newly made tool. If you are making a script then that script should do one thing well and if you need to do multiple things then make another and then import both scripts into a common script where they can be used. Code refactorization is also important for maintenance because it means that clean up the code that you’ve written to make sure that it is simple, professional, and elegant. Oftentimes this means that you make rewrite an object so that it is easier to understand when you hand it to someone else or try to write documentation for it. This may mean splitting things up so that they are more general and act more like Lego blocks than welded parts.

Refactor means that code is adjusted to work more flexibly while still retaining its intended functionality. Note: this may involve taking a less optimized approach that it more understand and more flexible while understanding the limitations of the code.

Code testing is a major point that I want to harp on because it is not talked about enough in teaching python. This is when you implement tests/logic to make sure that your code is robust and you can figure out what went wrong if your code doesn’t work right. This solves a debugging problem by giving diagnostics about what failed and why when you test a software application. unit testing is a specific tool that has been transformed into a methodology called Test-Driven Development. The idea is that you can create simple tests that will tell you if your code is operating the way you want by seeing if the results you pass are as expected or if they are different. This is useful when your code has bugs that don’t result in errors so you end up with a software that is telling you false information that is assumed to be right.

X = 1

y = x + x

y = 1000

Integration testing helps to make sure that when various pieces of code, imported modules, and called services all work together as expected. Note that pieces of code, modules, and services can operate without error while still delivering faulty, buggy results. These are more computer intensive than unit tests since it means that various parts of the code will be initialized and then tested. This is crucial for making sure that your code works the way it is supposed to with other code. This only tests whether the pieces work together not if they work together well. Functional testing is testing to focus on how the software accomplishes the business requirements that it was designed to accomplish. If a search app was designed then this kind of testing determine whether people can effectively search from a business or use perspective to accomplish the requirement of enabling people to search effectively. This tests to see if pieces work together well and correctly. End-to-end testing is to test specific use cases that would imitate a user trying to perform some action that is often more complex than simply testing functionality. These kinds of tests are useful but hard to maintain and should not be relied on since this changes often and it hard to develop without existing test infrastructure.

The third major problem that developers face is Code communication which is when more than one person is working on code but everyone has to understand what is happening. The question is then how do you make sure that your change won’t screw up the codebase? Consider the fact that multiple people may be working on different functions that are going to placed in the same document. How can you make sure that the solution that you’ve made still works? By using source control and version control like Github, we can solve this problem. source control is important to make sure that the foundation multiple people are building on stays the same. Consider a team of architects decides to work with contractors to build a house. If one architect goes in the middle of the night and changes the plans then this may affect whether the solutions that other architects made will apply. Additionally, the contractors will have to completely redo their work since their solution may no longer be valid. If changes are understood and agreed upon by the entire team then this problem can be averted. This is done by having people copies of an agreed upon assumption/framework and then putting their solution on top. The various solutions are combined and then any errors that result can be resolved though this should be minimal in an ideal case. Another problem is versioning because people may not know what the latest code is. By implementing a versioning tool, people can ensure that they have the latest setup and along with knowing how changes were implemented over various iterations.

The last major problem that developers face is code comprehension. This is common because people often jump to asking ChatGPT or searching Stack Overflow for the answer rather than deducing the answer on their own. This can save time but it comes at the expense of understanding and exercise of intellectual faculties which need to be tested and stressed constantly so that we can grow. The first symptom of this is poor documentation. Documentation is crucial for making sure that people can understand your code if they want to go back and understand. Good code is something that people love to go back and use, including yourself. Consider the library OpenCV which has a famously amazing documentation which can walk anyone through how to do object recognition. Below I’ve listed the various kids of documentation. I would recommend looking up some examples. I hope to update this essay with my own example someday.

  1. one-liner documentation : This is when you just put small comments next to your statements to help elucidate what the goal of your command is. This can help you think through what you want to do along with guiding others.
  2. function-level documentation: This is documentation that is placed at the top of a series of one-liners. It explains what the overall goal of the following commands is as well as how to use the function. The function can be implemented as a one-liner documentation so we want to understand how to use the function easily but don’t want to read through the details of what happens.
  3. class-level documentation: This is documentation that explains what the set of functions/methods is designed to do and what the goal of this collection of functions/methods is. It also explains what the initialization of this class does and how to use it. This should be a higher level description than a compilation of function-level documentation. It should explain how to use the class and the available functions with brief descriptions of what they are for and how to use them.

  4. script-level documentation: This is documentation that is designed to explain what the point of the script/library is. This is a high level view of what the code module does and it explains any classes, script-level functions, and script-wide parameters. This allows someone who calls the module into another document to understand what functionality they can gain and what tools are available to do so. This can be something with a summary followed by a fairly lengthy detailed description that shows what the code can do on a functional, goal-oriented level. reasoning: This means applying logic and understanding the cognitive train of thought that it involved with getting from one set of information or assumptions to a conclusion. Reasoning often occurs in a passive sense and it is something that we do fast-thinking; however, something reasoning involves slow-thinking. We can use models to simplify the logical sequence of steps that must be taken to understand a conclusion. This is often expensive to do in reality and it may not be feasible with additional time or cognitive constraints. This can be improved by developing familiarity with reading documentation. Reading documentation can be tedious but repeated exposure and application can create fast-thinking frameworks that enable the ability to understand how code works faster. Additionally, looking at the definition of the variable, function, class, or script that is being called and see how it is defined within the codebase. This means trying to see what the object does and how it works by looking at the way that some has created ie. look at where the function is defined and read through and understand how it works. VS Code offers an easy way to do this through peeking or simply going to the object definition. Another way to reason through code and understand it is to find something that is easily understood and then trace the cognitive steps backwards to the beginning. Do this multiple times like peeling the layers of an onion. Third, find quality examples that provide good exposure to the principles and assumptions at play. This will force you to integrate the ideas into your mental model. This can be done through intellectus or more rigorously through ratio. intellectus will allow for a fast-thinking model to detect patterns; however, it will create patterns that may or may not be present. Last is to find CS patterns rather than learning Syntax: Oftentimes, when learning to get started in programming. One has a tendency to imitate and copy the work that has been established before. By learning CS patterns then we can learn principles that can be readily and quickly applied to develop new things. This allows ratio. Another way that code comprehension fails it that people don’t practice by doing and playing. Observation/contemplation is when we simply see the code running and we look at the outputs and see what happens when the program is run. It doesn’t imply that you have strong deductive knowledge about how the program works only that you know how to use it. The use of observation allows us to gain knowledge that the experts have and use, but are unable to convey as a result of hidden assumptions. Exposing these hidden assumptions consciously takes a lot of work and therefore it may be easier to implement a habit of observation. This is what happens in art.

    Try implementing some of the solutions below:

  5. Practice, Practice, Practice: One should practice regularly and ingest as much hands-on learning as possible to develop experience and familiarity with programming. Otherwise, there is no real understanding of causality and it can lead to faulty mental model.
  6. Experiment with failure: Try to see how something will fail and how it will work based on how you interact with the object.
  7. Find quality examples: This means making sure the examples and practices you observe are quality. Sometimes it is appropriate to accept or learn a bad practice so that appreciation can be obtained for the right way.

Lastly code comprehension fails because people don’t take the time to find help and appeal to authority. This is when you consult a trusted person or resource like Stack Overflow to determine what is happening. This can also be through reading through the documentation for any functions which is almost always available. Don’t be afraid to ask online and in-person: The first step to learning is accepting the role of a student and then next is being a good one. One tip is to post questions regularly on forms and discussion boards. Resources like Stack Overflow are great for finding solutions while learning something new. Other stack exchange websites can be used as well. Second, read documentation. This means that you take the time necessary to learn something and then integrate as part of your mental model for creating a solution. Third, is to maintain awareness by consistently keeping up with how understanding is being developed and applied throughout the programming community. This means signing up for blogs, email lists, and conferences. They can offer the ability to update who one should appeal to for authority.

entry.title: Welcome to Jekyll!
entry.content:
You’ll find this post in your _posts directory. Go ahead and edit it and re-build the site to see your changes. You can rebuild the site in many different ways, but the most common way is to run jekyll serve, which launches a web server and auto-regenerates your site when a file is updated.

Jekyll requires blog post files to be named according to the following format:

YEAR-MONTH-DAY-title.MARKUP

Where YEAR is a four-digit number, MONTH and DAY are both two-digit numbers, and MARKUP is the file extension representing the format used in the file. After that, include the necessary front matter. Take a look at the source for this post to get an idea about how it works.

Jekyll also offers powerful support for code snippets:

Check out the Jekyll docs for more info on how to get the most out of Jekyll. File all bugs/feature requests at Jekyll’s GitHub repo. If you have questions, you can ask them on Jekyll Talk.
